title: Traffic model handoff + benchmark scoping
summary: Handoff of customer traffic model and initial benchmark acceptance criteria. Agreed to run three canonical runs (baseline batch, streaming low-latency, and spike tolerance) using customer scripts + Redwood adapter. Main risks: live KV cache differences, tokenization mismatches, and network egress shaping. Next: Redwood to provide harness adapter + example traffic.json, customer to produce sanitized script subset and sample traces.
action_items: Marco Diaz (Redwood SE): Share prototype harness adapter and README (2026-11-24)
Jenna Lee (Customer PM): Upload sanitized customer scripts + two 1-hour sample traces to shared drive (2026-11-25)
Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Send preliminary pricing band and pilot contract draft (2026-11-26)
Omar Khan (Customer SRE): Provide current infra egress ip list and expected concurrency profile (2026-11-24)
Priya Singh (Customer ML): Prepare 50 sample prompts and success eval script (2026-11-27)
next_steps: Redwood will push adapter repo link and lightweight runner image.
Customer will mark 3 priority endpoints and provide golden outputs for quality checks.
Schedule benchmark kickoff (1 hour) week of 2026-11-29 to validate baseline run.
Agree on pass/fail thresholds and telemetry tags before runs.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-21
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Leah Park (CS), Jenna Lee (BrightCart PM), Omar Khan (SRE), Priya Singh (Lead ML), Evan Ross (Dev)

Summary: Handoff and scoping for benchmark runs using customer scripts. Discussed streaming vs batch, workload shape, acceptance criteria, and deliverables.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — I think we have the right folks. Marco and I will lead the benchmark scoping, Leah's on for success metrics and admin. Jenna, want to kick us off with the traffic profile?

[00:18] Jenna (BrightCart PM): Yeah hi, quick context. We're BrightCart — commerce search, personalized recs. For POC we want to validate two things: 1) steady-state throughput at our normal load which is around 1.2k qps across 50 nodes, and 2) tail/peak handling for flash sales where we see 5-7x spikes. Most of our requests are short prompts, like 80-160 tokens, some multi-turn dialogs for support flow.

[00:40] Omar (SRE): Just to add the concurrency -- typical concurrency per instance is 12 requests in flight, but during flash events we go up to ~80. Our top concern is cold-start tail latency and also CPU egress shaping since we're in a VPC with strict firewall egress.

[01:00] Marco (Redwood SE): Got it. A couple clarifying q's — when you say "scripts" are you talking about actual production SDK calls we can replay, or sanitized offline traces? We need something that reproduces client-side streaming behavior if you want low-latency streaming runs.

[01:18] Jenna: We'll provide sanitized SDK call traces. Evan will be point for that. For streaming we currently do chunked input — we stream tokens from the browser to backend, model streaming needs to match our chunk size.

[01:30] Evan (Dev): yeah, we do 64-token chunks for most streaming flows. Batch jobs are different, they take batched user groups at off-peak windows.

[01:42] Marco: Perfect. For the benchmark we recommend three canonical runs: baseline batch (non-streaming, steady-state), streaming low-latency (simulate 64-token chunk streaming), and spike tolerance (sudden RPS increase with cold kv-cache evictions). Each run should be instrumented for p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost-per-1k tokens.

[02:05] Priya (Lead ML): Quick question on quality checks — we'll need to compare outputs to golden set for acceptance. How do you handle tokenization diffs and small nonlinearities in outputs? We don't want to fail due to benign paraphrases.

[02:20] Marco: Good point. Our acceptance harness supports fuzzy matching and ROUGE/BLEU-style thresholds. For generation-sensitive endpoints we recommend edit-distance or embedding similarity > 0.88 as pass, and for classification-like outputs exact match or top-1. We'll work with your Priya on thresholds.

[02:37] Alex: Also to flag, depending on whether you choose Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, the baseline cost and latency expectations will shift. Since you're network-constrained, Dedicated in-region or Private VPC is often better for tail latency but has setup time. Any preference?

[02:55] Omar: We're leaning Private for compliance — all logs must stay in our VPC. But for the POC we can tolerate a hosted pilot if we can run in a peered VPC and get egress IPs. Time to first run is a factor, though.

[03:12] Leah (CS): For clarity, the POC acceptance can be done on hosted with VPC peering; if the numbers look good, we then propose a Dedicated pilot or Private deploy for the longer engagement.

[03:26] Jenna: Timeline wise we'd like benchmarks complete within two weeks so we can make a Q4 run decision. Is that realistic?

[03:34] Marco: Two weeks is tight but feasible if scripts and sample traces are available this week. First step is adapter + runner from Redwood; second step is a dry-run to validate telemetry mapping; third step is full benchmark. If any dev work needed to sanitize scripts, that can be the blocker.

[03:53] Evan: Our main blocker is scrubbing PII and tying down tokens; we can probably produce a sanitized subset by Wednesday if you provide the script format.

[04:04] Marco: We'll send an example traffic.json and adapter README today. Our adapter will accept an array of events with fields: timestamp, client_id, prompt, stream_chunks (optional), expected_response_id. Note: that's the adapter schema, not production code.

[04:20] Priya: A note on metrics — we need to capture per-request KV cache hit ratio, per-token micro-latencies, and overall cost. Can Redwood expose those?

[04:30] Marco: Yes we can emit tags: redwood.kv_hit, redwood.sequence_len, redwood.quant_profile, and integration will make these available in the trace export. Small caveat: if you're using your on-prem KV and we run hosted, KV semantics differ; cache warmup behavior will not be identical.

[04:50] Omar: That's one of the risks we flagged. For the spike run we want cache cold-start scenario to be realistic. How do you model that?

[04:58] Marco: We can run with explicit cache flush between iterations and then drive a sudden RPS ramp to measure cold-start tail. We'll also do a warm run to compare.

[05:10] Jenna: On success criteria — propose p95 < 250ms for streaming tokens, p99 < 850ms, and quality similarity >= 0.88. Cost target TBD based on your pricing band. Does that map to what Redwood usually sees?

[05:25] Alex: Those p95/p99 targets are ambitious but achievable with right placement and quantization. If you need NVMe-backed KV or pinned Dedicated GPUs, p99s improve. We'll map cost targets after we present pricing.

[05:40] Marco: Regarding quantization — if you want lower cost, we can test INT8 variants. Warning: some generation outputs shift slightly, so you need to validate with Priya's quality checks. We'll include quantized runs as an optional axis.

[06:00] Priya: Good. We'll add quantized run acceptance rules.

[06:05] Evan: One implementation question — we use long context for session continuity in chat; is your harness going to preserve KV cache across simulated sessions?

[06:15] Marco: Yes, adapter supports session id mapping and will warm kv per session. Two modes: isolated (flush every request) or session-persistent (keep KV for N requests). We'll need you to indicate which endpoints need persistence.

[06:31] Jenna: Search endpoints are mostly stateless; support chat flows are persistent. We'll flag them in the artifacts.

[06:40] Leah: I'm going to log that as a dependency — customer to flag persistence endpoints.

[06:48] Omar: Security question — we'll need SOC2 and encryption docs before we run anything with real traces. Can you attach those?

[06:56] Alex: Absolutely. I'll attach SOC 2 type II summary, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integration notes. For hosted peered runs we'll share a minimal set of logs; full audit logs are available with Dedicated/Private.

[07:10] Jenna: Also, do you support client-side streaming via websocket, or is it only long-poll? We need to mimic the exact client behaviour to measure frontend latency.

[07:21] Marco: Our runner supports websocket replay and chunked streaming. We'll need a small shim in the adapter to map your chunk boundaries; most customers use our default chunk handler but you can provide your chunk frame size.

[07:34] Evan: We'll give chunk size and sample streams.

[07:40] Priya: A quick ask on telemetry labels — can you add a tag for our internal feature flag so we can split results by experiment?

[07:48] Marco: Sure, include 'brightcart.feature' as a tag in the traffic.json and we'll preserve it in traces.

[07:55] Alex: Wrapping to acceptance criteria — re-state: 3 canonical runs, agreed success thresholds, golden output comparisons, and cost delta within X% of benchmark. Jenna, you ok with that?

[08:06] Jenna: Yes that sounds right. Question: for the spike run, do you simulate external network shaping? Because our traffic goes through an egress firewall that adds jitter.

[08:18] Marco: We can simulate egress shaping client-side via the runner (introduce latency/jitter). If you can provide distributions from your monitoring, we can replay it.

[08:29] Omar: We'll share a histogram of outbound latency during peak.

[08:32] Leah: I'll collect that with Evan and attach.

[08:37] Alex: Any competitor parity checks you want us to run? Sometimes customers ask for a quick compare vs Anthropic small for latency and vs their internal on-prem model for quality.

[08:48] Priya: If it's cheap, run a single-sample compare to Anthropic base for latency, but don't over-index. Quality baseline is our on-prem small model.

[08:58] Marco: Noted. We'll do a one-off latency baseline against Anthropic small as a head-to-head.

[09:07] Evan: On the adapter — what's the form of the runner image? Do we need to host a container or you provide?

[09:13] Marco: We'll share a lightweight Docker image and a small Kubernetes job manifest for you to run in your environment if you prefer. Alternatively, we can run hosted and stream telemetry back. If you want Private parity, customer-run is preferable.

[09:27] Jenna: For the POC we'll prefer Redwood-hosted with VPC peering to speed things up, then run a customer-hosted verification if results look good.

[09:36] Alex: Great. Last bit — deliverables and dates: Marco shares adapter by 11/24, Jenna uploads sanitized scripts by 11/25, kickoff run week of 11/29. Any objections?

[09:49] Priya: No objections. A small ask — include a sample evaluation notebook so our ML team can reproduce scores locally.

[09:58] Marco: Will do. We'll include a Jupyter notebook and an example scoring harness.

[10:06] Omar: And please include IP allowlist for the hosted runner so we can open firewall as needed.

[10:12] Alex: We'll provide egress IPs.

[10:16] Jenna: Okay, sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[10:20] Alex: Quick recap of next steps — I'll send pricing and security docs, Marco will push adapter and runner, Jenna/Evan will share sanitized traces and scripts, Omar will provide egress histogram and IP list, Priya will build golden outputs and evaluation rules. We'll meet for the kickoff the week of 11/29.

[10:38] (crosstalk)

[10:45] Leah: I'll create the shared folder and calendar invite for the kickoff.

[10:50] Jenna: Thanks, that's all from us.

[10:54] Alex: Appreciate it. We'll follow up with the links. Bye everyone.

End of call.
